title: Filling the low brackets
teaches: Why low-income years are worth using on purpose: Roth conversions and 0 percent gains up to the top of a bracket, how the two compete for the same space, and what filling saves over a lifetime

blocks.text: A couple, both born in 1966, stops work at 60 in 2026 with $600,000 in a taxable account, $1.2 million in traditional 401(k)s and IRAs, and $200,000 in Roth accounts. They spend $80,000 a year and will claim $50,000 a year of Social Security at 67. The usual advice is to spend the taxable account first, then the pre-tax accounts, and leave the Roth for last. Followed to the letter, it gives them seven years with almost no federal income tax: they live on share sales, mostly **basis**, the money they first paid for the shares, which comes back untaxed, and the rest gains in the 0 percent band.

It sounds ideal, and it is one of the most expensive mistakes in retirement planning. While they pay nothing, the $1.2 million in pre-tax accounts keeps growing. For anyone born in 1960 or later, the law requires withdrawals from it every year from 75, and by then, growing at 4 percent a year after inflation, it is about $2.2 million.[^rmd] Their first required withdrawal is about $88,000, on top of $50,000 of Social Security, and both rise from there. The brackets they left empty in their sixties are gone for good; the tax arrives later, at higher rates.

The alternative is to use the empty years on purpose: each year, move enough from the pre-tax accounts into a Roth, or take enough as income, to fill the 10 and 12 percent brackets. What follows works out how much to move, and what gets in the way.

Think of each year's low brackets as space that expires on 31 December. A couple's standard deduction is $32,200 of space taxed at 0 percent. The 10 and 12 percent brackets then run up to $100,800 of taxable income, which is $133,000 of ordinary income once the deduction is added back. Any ordinary income placed in that space costs at most 12 percent, and the space can't be carried into next year.

Two things want the space: Roth conversions and long-term gains. Gains are taxed at 0 percent only while taxable income stays under the $98,900 line, the top of the 0 percent band, and lesson 7 showed that ordinary income goes underneath and pushes them out. So a couple living on gains who also converts pays twice for the same space: 12 percent on the conversion, plus 15 percent on each dollar of gains pushed up. Guess, then see it.

blocks.caption: A married couple living on long-term gains from a taxable account converts some pre-tax money to a Roth. Above: the federal tax the conversion adds. Below: the rate on the next $1,000 converted. The dashed line is the top of the 12 percent bracket.
blocks.task: Guess, then try small and large gains

blocks.text: With no gains, a conversion's cost rises by the brackets alone: nothing for the first $32,200, then 10 percent, then 12, then 22. With $40,000 of gains, there is a stretch where each extra dollar converted costs 27 percent, even though the couple never leaves the 12 percent bracket. With large gains the stretch widens.

The choice between the two isn't obvious. Gains realised at 0 percent never pay tax: sell the shares and buy them straight back, and the new, higher price becomes the basis, so those gains are wiped off the books for good.[^reset] A conversion moves money that will otherwise be taxed later, probably at 12 or 22 percent. Many plans do both but avoid mixing them in the same year, since the mix is what costs 27 percent: in years with little ordinary income, realise gains up to the top of the 0 percent band; in years when gains are small, convert to the top of the 12 percent bracket.

The course's household model runs the couple from 60 to 95 with each strategy: spending, tax, required withdrawals, Social Security, and growth of 4 percent a year after inflation. Filling to the top of the 12 percent bracket means drawing or converting pre-tax money each year until ordinary taxable income reaches $100,800, spending what's needed and converting the rest.

blocks.caption: The same couple from 60 to 95 under three withdrawal plans, from the course's household model. Federal income tax only.

blocks.text: Leaving the low brackets empty costs this couple about $385,000 in federal tax over their lives. Filling to the top of 12 percent costs about $160,000, and leaves their heirs some $780,000 more after tax. That is more than the $225,000 of tax saved, because the money moved early grows untaxed in the Roth for decades, and heirs inherit a Roth without owing income tax on it, while the model charges them tax on inherited pre-tax money. Filling to the top of 22 percent pays more tax than filling to 12, because it pays 22 percent on dollars that would otherwise have come out at 12.

Before 65, though, this couple buys health insurance on the ACA marketplace, and the government's help with the premiums, the premium credits of lesson 11, shrinks as income rises. Filling to 12 percent here pushes them past the income at which credits stop (four times the poverty line, about $85,000 for a couple in 2026), so they lose about $68,000 of credits over five years, which they pay in premiums instead. Filling still wins, but by less, and a plan that keeps income under the line until 65 and fills harder afterwards may do better. Lesson 11 takes this apart.

Fill up to the top of the bracket whose rate matches the rate you expect the money to pay later, counting everything. As in lesson 8, the calculation comes down to four things: how big required withdrawals will be at 75, how much Social Security will arrive and when, whether one spouse will be widowed and filing alone with half the brackets,[^widow] and whether heirs will inherit pre-tax money in their own peak earning years.

Running the model on other households gives a few rough rules. Filling the 12 percent bracket usually pays for anyone with pre-tax savings well above $500,000. Filling into 22 percent tends to pay mainly for pre-tax balances of $2 million or more, or for a couple whose survivor will face single brackets for many years. Filling to 24 percent and beyond rarely pays outside very large estates. The branch on taxable accounts and the capstone, lesson 14, let you try your own numbers.

A few details affect the timing. Convert soon after markets have fallen, rather than waiting for year end: the shares moved are cheap, so a dollar of tax moves more shares into the Roth, and their recovery happens there, tax-free. Count on Social Security taxation (lesson 12) once benefits start, which can make the next dollar cost about 22 percent inside the 12 percent bracket, and about 40 percent inside the 22. And plan in advance for 63 and 64, whose income sets Medicare premiums two years later (lesson 12).

blocks.title: Hold on to
points: Low brackets left empty in early retirement can't be used later; required withdrawals arrive at 73 or 75 and fill them for you, at higher rates.
Roth conversions and 0 percent gains compete for the same space; mixing them can cost 27 percent inside the 12 percent bracket.
For the sample couple, filling to the top of 12 percent cut lifetime federal tax from about $385,000 to $160,000.
The right top is the rate the money would pay later, counting required withdrawals, Social Security and a surviving spouse.

blocks.caption: Six questions on filling the brackets
blocks.task: Choose the best answer to each

items.ask: Why can living only on a taxable account in early retirement turn out expensive?
choices: The pre-tax accounts keep growing, and required withdrawals later fill the brackets at higher rates
Taxable accounts are taxed at 37 percent
The basis is lost after ten years
items.why: Years of near-zero income waste the low brackets, while the pre-tax balance grows into large required withdrawals at 73 or 75.

items.ask: A couple with no other income converts $100,000 to a Roth in 2026. What is the federal tax?
items.why: $32,200 is covered by the standard deduction; of the remaining $67,800, the first $24,800 is taxed at 10 percent and the rest at 12: $2,480 + $5,160 = $7,640.

items.ask: A couple has $40,000 of gains and is converting inside the 12 percent bracket. Why can the next dollar converted cost 27 percent?
choices: It is taxed at 12 percent and pushes a dollar of gains from 0 to 15 percent
The 12 percent bracket ends at the 0 percent gains line
items.why: Ordinary income goes underneath the gains, so each dollar converted moves a dollar of gains above the 0 percent line.

items.ask: What happens to gains realised in the 0 percent band?
choices: They are never taxed, because the basis rises to the sale price
They are taxed later when the money is spent
They are added to next year's income
items.why: Selling and buying back raises the basis, so those gains are permanently free of tax.

items.ask: For the sample couple, roughly how much federal tax did filling to the top of the 12 percent bracket save over their lives?
choices: Nothing; it only moved tax around
items.why: About $385,000 with the low brackets left empty against about $160,000 with them filled.

items.ask: Which makes filling into the 22 percent bracket more worthwhile?
choices: A pre-tax balance in the millions
items.why: Large pre-tax balances mean large required withdrawals later, which land in 22 percent or above anyway.

summary: **Unused low brackets expire every year.** Space left empty can't be used later, while untouched pre-tax accounts grow into large required withdrawals at 73 or 75.
**Roth conversions and 0 percent gains compete.** Both use the same bracket space, and mixing them can cost 27 percent inside the 12 percent bracket.
**Filling the 12 percent bracket usually pays.** It can cut a couple's lifetime federal tax by more than half, while filling 22 percent pays only with large pre-tax balances.
**Before 65, lost health credits count too.** Premium credits lost to higher income can eat much of what filling a bracket saves.

rmd.title: Required minimum distributions
rmd.text: From the age set by law, 73 for people born from 1951 to 1959 and 75 for those born in 1960 or later, a share of each pre-tax account must be withdrawn each year: the balance at the end of the previous year divided by a life-expectancy figure from the IRS's Uniform Lifetime Table, 24.6 at 75. Roth accounts have no required withdrawals during the owner's life.

reset.title: Selling to reset the basis
reset.text: To realise a gain at 0 percent, sell shares and buy them straight back. The wash-sale rule, which stops you claiming a loss if you buy back within 30 days, doesn't apply to gains. The new basis is the price paid on the day, so future gains are measured from there. It only helps in a taxable account; inside a 401(k) or IRA there is no basis to reset.

widow.title: The survivor's brackets
widow.text: After one spouse dies, the survivor files as a single person (after the year of death, unless there is a dependent child). A single filer's standard deduction and 10, 12, 22 and 24 percent brackets are exactly half a married couple's, while required withdrawals from the combined pre-tax accounts stay just as large and only the smaller of the two Social Security benefits stops.
